Tactile 3D print

Download an STL of the mountain to print and explore by touch. Routes stand up as smooth, rounded ridges. Each risk class has its own sharp-edged pattern so it never feels like the natural terrain: Low is smooth, Moderate has diagonal ribs, Considerable has round flat-topped studs, High has square pyramids and Extreme has tall, tightly packed spikes. The texture follows the conditions set in the Conditions tab at the moment you download. Preview print shows the exact model on the map before you download it.

A touch legend runs along the south edge. From west to east it has five texture patches from Low to Extreme, marked with one to five raised dots, then a smooth ridge showing how a route feels.

Heights are exaggerated 1.5 times on a 3 mm base. Route ridges are 2.2 mm wide and 2.2 mm tall, above the tallest texture. Print with a 0.4 mm nozzle at 0.12 to 0.16 mm layers so the texture survives.
Raised routes
Select a route in the Routes tab to add it. Your drawn routes and the safest route are included when they exist.

What the map shows

Each 30 m cell gets a relative risk index from 0 to 100. It combines how likely an avalanche is to start there or reach there (terrain), how unstable the snowpack is (conditions), and how bad the outcome would be (consequence). It is a comparison tool, not a probability.

The map is a 3D model of the elevation data, drawn as a 60 m mesh with no vertical exaggeration. The risk or ATES layer, 100 m contours and hillshade are draped over it at 15 m detail.

Terrain layers (pre-computed)

  • Elevation: USGS 3DEP 1 arc-second DEM, resampled to a 30 m grid over about 12.5 × 14.5 km around Mount Temple.
  • Release areas: fuzzy slope membership peaking near 40° (about 0.5 at 29° and 51°), reduced on very rough terrain and below treeline.
  • Runout exposure: energy-line propagation downhill from release areas using a 24° travel angle above treeline and 28° below (forest friction proxy). This catches valley floors and lakeshores under big slopes.
  • Terrain traps: gullies (concave curvature), cliffs (>50°), and abrupt flats below steep slopes.
  • ATES class: simplified AutoATES-style rules: Simple, Challenging, Complex, Extreme from slope angle, release areas, runout overlap and cliffs.

Last 60 days of weather

  • For the selected date the app pulls the 61 days of hourly weather before it for Mount Temple from Open-Meteo: current forecast models for recent dates, archived forecast models from 2022, ERA5 reanalysis before that. ERA5 precipitation is also pulled and averaged with the model, because the two disagreed by about three times in autumn 2026 (21 mm against 62 mm). If today's pull fails it uses the snapshot saved in the page and says so.
  • Parks Canada weather stations (via Avalanche Canada, from 2024): snow depth at Bosworth Lower (2210 m, treeline) and Stanley (1930 m, below treeline) replaces the modelled depth and gives daily new snow; ridgetop wind from Bosworth Upper (2745 m, Whymper as backup) replaces the model wind; the model's temperature is shifted by its average error against Bosworth Upper; alpine snowfall is scaled by how far off the model was at treeline.
  • The Parks Canada forecast for the selected date sets the danger ratings and problems when one was issued (archive from 2023). Mountain Information Network reports within 20 km are listed for context but do not change the score.
  • The single weather point is moved to three band elevations (below treeline 1850 m, treeline 2175 m, alpine 2700 m) with a −6.5 °C/km lapse rate and +50 % precipitation per km. Precipitation falls as snow below 0 °C, rain above +2 °C, mixed in between.
  • Each day and band: snow depth (new snow at about 1 cm per mm of water, 3 % daily settlement, degree-day melt), snow available for wind transport, and cold dry days on a thin snowpack (faceting).
  • For each band and each of 8 aspects a day counts as loading when it reaches a threshold: 30 cm storm snow in 72 h, 20 cm wind-deposited snow on lee aspects (wind over 20 km/h moving recent snow), 10 mm rain on a 30 cm snowpack, or strong warming on sunny aspects.
  • Recent loading = strongest loading in the last days, counted 100 % today, 80 % yesterday, 60 % two days ago and so on. It multiplies the hazard on that band and aspect by up to 2.1×. Thin snowpack (under about 20 cm) lowers hazard to about a third, because there is not enough snow to slide.
  • When Parks Canada issued no rating (early or late season, or before 2023) the app models one from the replay and marks it as modelled.

Buried weak layers

  • The model runs day by day from 1 October of the season (or 61 days back in summer) so layers buried before the 60-day window are kept.
  • Surface hoar: a clear night (Open-Meteo cloud cover under 20 %), light wind and a cold night at that elevation, with no new snow. Near-surface facets: a clear, cold night with little recent snow. Crusts: rain on snow, or melting on sunny slopes. Facets near the ground: a strong temperature gradient (ground at 0 °C) through a thin, cold snowpack for several days.
  • A layer is buried once enough new snow falls on it, then settles with the snowpack. It counts as a persistent slab problem between two burial depths and as deep persistent beyond, and fades with age or after a warm spell.
  • The night-time thresholds and burial depths are tuned against Parks Canada's problem lists (see Accuracy test). The layers are modelled, not observed.

Accuracy test

Exposure time

  • Travel time uses the Munter calculation: 1 km of distance or 100 m of climb or descent is one unit, at 4 units an hour uphill and 6 downhill, or half that in deep snow or on snowshoes.
  • Minutes in start zones (release potential above 0.45) and under slopes (runout reach 0.25 or more) are added up. Risk-weighted exposure multiplies each minute by the score at that spot.
  • Warming: on the selected day, when the hourly air temperature at that elevation is above 0 °C and the sun is out, the score on sunny slopes is raised by up to 1.8×. This rule is a simplification; the test checks the daily version against days Parks Canada listed wet avalanche problems.

Conditions model

  • Danger rating for each elevation band (BTL < 2000 m, TL 2000–2350 m, ALP > 2350 m) scales hazard roughly ×2 per level, following the Avalanche Canada scale.
  • Avalanche problems raise hazard on the listed aspects and bands (likelihood and size) and lower it elsewhere. Persistent and deep persistent problems extend runout weight. Loose problems shorten it. Cornices add hazard on crests.
  • Weather now: new snow loads all aspects above the freezing level. Wind over 15 km/h loads lee aspects near ridge crests. Warming above 0 °C adds hazard on sunny aspects and below the freezing level.

Formula

terrain = 1 − (1 − release) × (1 − 0.85 × runout)
season = (1 + 0.7 × recent loading + 0.35 × facets) × (0.35 + 0.65 × snowpack support)
raw = terrain × danger × problem × weather × season × (1 + 0.6 × trap)
index = 100 × (1 − e^(−1.4 × raw))

Classes: Low < 14, Moderate 14–31, Considerable 31–55, High 55–78, Extreme ≥ 78.

3D print

The STL is built in the browser from the same elevation data at about 0.4 mm spacing, with heights exaggerated 1.5 times. The risk class, from the index smoothed over 150 m, sets a geometric texture with hard edges: diagonal ribs 0.6 mm tall for Moderate, flat-topped studs 0.9 mm tall on a 3.2 mm grid for Considerable, square pyramids 1.2 mm tall for High and staggered spikes 1.5 mm tall on a 2.4 mm grid for Extreme. Low is left smooth. Routes are smooth rounded ridges 2.2 mm tall, so a finger can follow them through the textured ground. The model is watertight with a flat base. A legend strip along the south edge holds one patch for each risk class, textured with that class's pattern and marked with one to five dots, plus a sample route ridge.

Route scoring

Routes are sampled every 15 m. Route score = 0.55 × 90th percentile + 0.45 × maximum, so one serious crux can't be averaged away by long safe sections. Cruxes are continuous stretches at Considerable or above.

Safest route

A* search over the 30 m grid. Step cost = distance × slope effort + uphill gain + slider weight × distance × (index/100)². Slopes over 48° are treated as impassable. The search finds the path with the lowest total cost.

Limitations

  • One weather point for the whole map. Terrain spreads it by elevation band and aspect only; local wind channelling around Temple is not modelled.
  • No snowpack layering. The faceting count is a rough flag, not a stability test, and buried weak layers from before the 60-day window are not seen.
  • The loading thresholds came from the earlier calibration on a synthetic mountain and have not been checked against Parks Canada observations at Lake Louise.
  • No forest-cover data: treeline effects come from elevation bands only.
  • Summer trails are scored on their summer line. Winter travel often takes different lines (for example frozen lakes and the valley floor), which can be drawn or loaded as GPX.
  • Trail lines come from OpenStreetMap. The last pitch to the Mount Temple summit has no OSM line and uses a least-effort terrain path.
  • 30 m cells miss small features like rolls, cornice edges and short gullies. Glaciers, seracs and crevasses on Temple's north face are not modelled.
  • No station sits in the Moraine Lake or Paradise Valley drainages: the nearest are 16 to 20 km north and west, so local snowfall differences are not captured.
  • Station readings only go back to 2024 and the archived forecasts to 2023. Older dates run on the weather model alone.
